questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.14, ISRO2015-42
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
If one uses straight two-way merge sort algorithm to sort the following elements in ascending order:

     $20, \ 47, \ 15, \ 8, \ 9, \ 4, \ 40, \ 30, \ 12, \ 17$

then the order of these elements after second pass of the algorithm is:

  1. $8, \ 9, \ 15, \ 20, \ 47, \ 4, \ 12, \ 17, \ 30, \ 40$

  2. $8, \ 15, \ 20, \ 47, \ 4, \ 9, \ 30, \ 40, \ 12, \ 17$

  3. $15, \ 20, \ 47, \ 4, \ 8, \ 9, \ 12, \ 30, \ 40, \ 17$

  4. $4, \ 8, \ 9, \ 15, \ 20, \ 47, \ 12, \ 17, \ 30, \ 40$

review.concept: Algorithms - Straight Two-Way Merge Sort Trace
review.notes: Iterative two-way merge sort pass 1 produces pairs [20,47], [8,15], [4,9], [30,40], [12,17]. Pass 2 merges adjacent pairs into [8,15,20,47], [4,9,30,40], [12,17]. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.16
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
If $n$ is a power of $2$, then the minimum number of multiplications needed to compute $a^n$ is

  1. $\log_2 n$
  2. $\sqrt n$
  3. $n-1$
  4. $n$

review.concept: Algorithms - Exponentiation by Squaring and Multiplication Bounds
review.notes: For n = 2^k, exponentiation by repeated squaring requires exactly k = log_2(n) multiplications. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.17
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is the most powerful parsing method?

  1. LL (1)
  2. Canonical LR
  3. SLR
  4. LALR

review.concept: Compiler Design - Relative Power and Expressiveness of Parsing Methods
review.notes: Canonical LR (CLR(1)) strictly subsumes LALR(1), SLR(1), and LL(1). Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.18, ISRO2016-53
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the join of a relation $R$ with a relation $S$. If $R$ has $m$ tuples and $S$ has $n$ tuples then the maximum and minimum sizes of the join respectively are

  1. $m+n$ and $0$
  2. $mn$ and $0$
  3. $m+n$ and $|m-n|$
  4. $mn$ and $m+n$

review.concept: Databases - Relational Join Cardinality Bounds
review.notes: Maximum join cardinality is Cartesian product mn (all match); minimum join cardinality is 0 (disjoint attributes). Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.19
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
The relational algebra expression equivalent to the following tuple calculus expression:

$\left\{t \mid t \in r \land \left(t[A] = 10 \land t[B]=20\right)\right\}$ is

  1. $\sigma_{(A=10 \lor B=20)} (r)$

  2. $\sigma_{(A=10)} (r) \cup \sigma_{(B=20)} (r)$

  3. $\sigma_{(A=10)} (r) \cap \sigma_{(B=20)} (r)$

  4. $\sigma_{(A=10)} (r) - \sigma_{(B=20)} (r)$

review.concept: Databases - Equivalence Between Tuple Relational Calculus and Relational Algebra
review.notes: Tuple calculus conjunction (A=10 and B=20) maps to intersection sigma_{A=10}(r) cap sigma_{B=20}(r). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.20
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Booth's coding in $8$ bits for the decimal number $-57$ is:

  1. $0-100+1000$
  2. $0-100+100-1$
  3. $0-1+100-10+1$
  4. $00-10+100-1$

review.concept: Digital Logic / Computer Arithmetic - Booth's Recoding Algorithm
review.notes: -57 in 8-bit two's complement is 11000111. Applying y_i = b_{i-1} - b_i with b_{-1}=0 yields 0 -1 0 0 +1 0 0 -1. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.21
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The maximum gate delay for any output to appear in an array multiplier for multiplying two $n$ bit numbers is

  1. $O(n^2)$
  2. $O(n)$
  3. $O(\log n)$
  4. $O(1)$

review.concept: Digital Logic - Array Multiplier Critical Path and Propagation Delay
review.notes: Array multiplier critical path spans O(n) adder stages vertically and horizontally, giving O(n) maximum gate delay. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.22
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
The main memory of a computer has $2\;\text{cm}$ blocks while the cache has $2\;\text{c}$ blocks. If the cache uses the set associative mapping scheme with $2$ blocks per set, then block $k$ of the main memory maps to the set:

  1. $(k \mod m)$ of the cache
  2. $(k \mod c)$ of the cache
  3. $(k \mod 2c)$ of the cache
  4. $(k \mod 2\; cm)$ of the cache

review.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Set-Associative Cache Mapping Function
review.notes: Cache has 2c blocks with 2 blocks/set, yielding 2c/2 = c sets. Block k maps to set k mod c. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.23
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
The Newton-Raphson method is to be used to find the root of the equation $f(x)=0$ where $x_o$ is the initial approximation and $f’$  is the derivative of $f$. The method converges

  1. always
  2. only if $f$ is a polynomial
  3. only if $f(x_o) <0$
  4. none of the above

review.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Convergence Properties of the Newton-Raphson Method
review.notes: Newton-Raphson convergence requires local curvature condition |f(x)f''(x)| < |f'(x)|^2, not polynomiality or f(x_0)<0, and does not hold unconditionally. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.24
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Let $R = (A, B, C, D, E, F)$ be a relation scheme with the following dependencies $C \rightarrow F, E \rightarrow A, EC \rightarrow D, A \rightarrow B $. Which one of the following is a key for $R$?

  1. CD
  2. EC
  3. AE
  4. AC

review.concept: Databases - Candidate Key Identification via Attribute Closure
review.notes: E and C never appear on RHS of any FD, so any key must contain EC. (EC)+ = {A,B,C,D,E,F} = R. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.25
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is correct?

  1. B-trees are for storing data on disk and B$^+$ trees are for main memory.

  2. Range queries are faster on B$^+$ trees.

  3. B-trees are for primary indexes and B$^+$ trees are for secondary indexes.

  4. The height of a B$^+$ tree is independent of the number of records.

review.concept: Databases - Comparison of B-Trees and B+ Trees
review.notes: In B+ trees, leaf nodes are linked sequentially, making range queries significantly faster with contiguous page scans compared to B-trees. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.6
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Let $L_1$ be the set of all languages accepted by a PDA by final state and $L_2$ the set of all languages accepted by empty stack. Which of the following is true?

  1. $L_1 = L_2$
  2. $L_1 \supset L_2$
  3. $L_1 \subset L_2$
  4. None

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Equivalence of PDA Acceptance Mechanisms
review.notes: PDA acceptance by final state and PDA acceptance by empty stack define the exact same class of languages (Context-Free Languages). Hence L1 = L2. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.4
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
If $L1$ is context free language and $L2$ is a regular language which of the following is/are false?

  1. $L1-L2$ is not context free

  2. $L1 \cap L2$ is context free

  3. $\sim L1$ is context free

  4. $\sim L2$ is regular

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Closure Properties of Context-Free and Regular Languages
review.notes: L1 - L2 = L1 cap ~L2 is always CFL, making statement A false. CFLs are not closed under complement, making statement C false. Statements B and D are true. False options are A and C. Matches official key [A, C].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.5
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
Given the programming constructs

  1. assignment
  2. for loops where the loop parameter cannot be changed within the loop
  3. if-then-else
  4. forward go to
  5. arbitrary go to
  6. non-recursive procedure call
  7. recursive procedure/function call
  8. repeat loop,

which constructs will you not include in a programming language such that it should be possible to program the terminates (i.e., halting) function in the same programming language

  1. $\text{(ii), (iii), (iv)}$
  2. $\text{(v), (vii), (viii)}$
  3. $\text{(vi), (vii), (viii)}$
  4. $\text{(iii), (vii), (viii)}$

review.concept: Theory of Computation / Programming Languages - Decidability of Program Termination and Language Sub-Recursiveness
review.notes: Arbitrary goto (v), recursive calls (vii), and repeat loops (viii) allow infinite loops. Excluding them ensures all programs terminate, making halting decidable. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.6
questions.subject: Unknown
questions.questionHtml:
For the schedule given below, which of the following is correct:
$\begin{array}{lll} \text{1} & \text{Read A} & \text{} \\ \text{2} & \text{} & \text{Read B} \\ \text{3} & \text{Write A} & \text{} \\ \text{4} & \text{} & \text{Read A} \\ \text{5} & \text{} & \text{Write A} \\ \text{6} & \text{} & \text{Write B} \\ \text{7} & \text{Read B} & \text{} \\ \text{8} & \text{Write B} & \text{} \\\end{array}$

  1. This schedule is serializable and can occur in a scheme using 2PL protocol
  2. This schedule is serializable but cannot occur in a scheme using 2PL protocol
  3. This schedule is not serializable but can occur in a scheme using 2PL protocol
  4. This schedule is not serializable and cannot occur in a scheme using 2PL protocol

review.concept: Databases - Serializability and Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol
review.notes: Conflicts produce cycle T1 -> T2 on A and T2 -> T1 on B, so schedule is not serializable. Since 2PL guarantees serializability, it cannot occur under 2PL. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.7, UGCNET-June2014-III: 25
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the schema $R=(S,T, U, V)$ and the dependencies $S \rightarrow T, T \rightarrow U, U \rightarrow V$ and $V \rightarrow S$. Let $R = (R1\text{ and } R2)$ be a decomposition such that $R1 \cap R2 \neq \phi$. The decomposition is

  1. not in $\textsf{2NF}$
  2. in $\textsf{2NF}$ but not $\textsf{3NF}$
  3. in $\textsf{3NF}$ but not in $\textsf{2NF}$
  4. in both $\textsf{2NF}$ and $\textsf{3NF}$

review.concept: Databases - Schema Decomposition and Normal Forms (2NF & 3NF)
review.notes: Since S, T, U, V all form candidate keys individually, all attributes are prime. With zero non-prime attributes, any decomposition is in both 2NF and 3NF. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.8
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the circuit shown below. In a certain steady state, the line $Y$ is at $'1'$. What are the possible values of $A, B$ and $C$ in this state?

  1. $A=0, B=0, C=1$

  2. $A=0, B=1, C=1$

  3. $A=1, B=0, C=1$

  4. $A=1, B=1, C=1$

review.concept: Digital Logic - Steady State Analysis of Sequential Feedback Circuits
review.notes: Circuit feedback analysis with steady state Y=1 aligns with official GATE 1999 key B (A=0, B=1, C=1).

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.9
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following sets of component(s) is/are sufficient to implement any arbitrary Boolean function?

  1. XOR gates, NOT gates

  2. $2$ to $1$ multiplexers

  3. AND gates, XOR gates

  4. Three-input gates that output $(A.B) + C$ for the inputs $A, B$ and $C$.

review.concept: Digital Logic - Functional Completeness of Gate Sets and Multiplexers
review.notes: 2-to-1 MUX is universal (implements NOT and AND). {AND, XOR} with constant 1 forms a complete Reed-Muller basis. {XOR, NOT} is purely linear, and AB+C is purely monotone (cannot invert). Matches official key [B, C].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.10
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
A multi-user, multi-processing operating system cannot be implemented on hardware that does not support

  1. Address translation
  2. DMA for disk transfer
  3. At least two modes of CPU execution (privileged and non-privileged)
  4. Demand paging

review.concept: Operating Systems - Hardware Support for Multi-User Multi-Processing Systems
review.notes: Multi-user OS requires dual execution modes (CPU protection) and address translation (memory protection). DMA and demand paging are performance/VM features. Matches official key [A, C].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.11
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is/are advantage(s) of virtual memory?

  1. Faster access to memory on an average.
  2. Processes can be given protected address spaces.
  3. Linker can assign addresses independent of where the program will be loaded in physical memory.
  4. Program larger than the physical memory size can be run.

review.concept: Operating Systems - Advantages and Characteristics of Virtual Memory
review.notes: Key advantages of virtual memory are executing programs larger than physical RAM (D) and isolating processes with protected address spaces (B). Memory access is never faster on average. Matches official key [B, D].

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.12
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following actions is/are typically not performed by the operating system when switching context from process $A$ to process $B$?

  1. Saving current register values and restoring saved register values for process $B$.
  2. Changing address translation tables.
  3. Swapping out the memory image of process $A$ to the disk.
  4. Invalidating the translation look-aside buffer.

review.concept: Operating Systems - Process Context Switching Actions and Overheads
review.notes: Context switching saves/restores registers, updates page table pointers, and flushes TLB, but never swaps memory to disk (which is an infrequent medium-term scheduler task). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.13
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following program in a language that has dynamic scooping:

var x: real;
procedure show:
    begin print(x);end;
procedure small;
    var x: real;
        begin x: = 0.125; show; end;
begin x:=0.25
    show; small
    end.

Then the output of the program is:

  1. 0.125 0.125
  2. 0.25 0.25
  3. 0.25 0.125
  4. 0.125 0.25

review.concept: Programming Languages - Dynamic Scoping and Variable Resolution
review.notes: Under dynamic scoping, show accesses x from its immediate caller on the stack: first from main (0.25), then from small (0.125). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.14
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
The number of tokens in the FORTRAN statement DO 10 I = 1.25 is

  1. 3
  2. 4
  3. 5
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Compiler Design - Lexical Analysis and FORTRAN Tokenization
review.notes: In fixed-format FORTRAN, spaces are ignored and the period makes 1.25 a real constant, turning the statement into an assignment DO10I = 1.25, which has exactly 3 tokens. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.15
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.questionHtml:
A grammar that is both left and right recursive for a non-terminal, is

  1. Ambiguous

  2. Unambiguous

  3. Information is not sufficient to decide whether it is ambiguous or unambiguous

  4. None of the above

review.concept: Compiler Design - Context-Free Grammars, Recursion, and Ambiguity
review.notes: Left and right recursion often causes ambiguity (e.g. E -> E+E) but does not guarantee it (e.g. unreachable non-terminals or disjoint sentential forms). Information is insufficient. Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.16
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The number of full and half-adders required to add $16$-bit numbers is

  1. $8$ half-adders, $8$ full-adders

  2. $1$ half-adder, $15$ full-adders

  3. $16$ half-adders, $0$ full-adders

  4. $4$ half-adders, $12$ full-adders

review.concept: Digital Logic - Binary Adder Architecture and Component Sizing
review.notes: Adding two 16-bit numbers uses 1 half-adder for the LSB (no carry-in) and 15 full-adders for the remaining positions. Matches official key B.
